title: Al-Ahad, the Unique
tomorrow: why does one Arabic word need a whole phrase in English?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Wahid, the One. The line: one. And a question: why would the Qur'an need both words, one and unique? A whole surah starts to answer it.

Everyone has a song on repeat, the one friends beg you to skip. In the time of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, a man had a surah like that. He was leading a group of travelers in prayer, and every time, whatever else he recited, he finished with the same short surah. Every prayer. The same few lines. His companions noticed. Then it started to bother them. When they came home, they told the Prophet. And the Prophet said: go and ask him why.
screen: `A SONG ON REPEAT.` → `THE SAME SURAH, EVERY PRAYER.` → `GO AND ASK HIM WHY.`

segments.voice: His answer, as Sahih al-Bukhari reports it, was simple: because it describes the Most Merciful, and I love to recite it. And the Prophet sent back word: tell him that Allah loves him. Here is the surah he couldn't stop saying, al-Ikhlas, in Pickthall's words: "Say: He is Allah, the One! Allah, the eternally Besought of all! He begetteth not nor was begotten. And there is none comparable unto Him." The word for One in that first line is ahad, and today's Name is Al-Ahad, the Unique. Yesterday's Name, Al-Wahid, says there is one. Some scholars hear Al-Ahad saying something more: one with no parts, nothing to divide, nothing beside Him to set Him next to. Which is why the surah ends where it does. Not with a number. With none comparable. Here's the detail to tell a friend tonight. Another report in Bukhari says this short surah is equal to a third of the Qur'an. Scholars explain that in different ways, and the report itself doesn't stop to say which. The man in the story didn't explain anything. He loved who the surah described, and that was enough for the Prophet to send him good news.
screen: `IT DESCRIBES THE MOST MERCIFUL.` · `TELL HIM ALLAH LOVES HIM.` · `AHAD: ONE WITH NO DIVISION.` · `EQUAL TO A THIRD OF THE QUR'AN.` · then, large: `UNIQUE.`

segments.voice: Say al-Ikhlas once, slowly and out loud: in Arabic if you know it, qul huwa Allahu ahad, or in Pickthall's English, He is Allah, the One. Then let the sit hold just that one word, ahad. When another thought walks in and stands next to it, the test, the group chat, tomorrow, notice it, let it go, and come back to the one word with nothing set beside it.
screen: `SAY IT ONCE, OUT LOUD.` · `QUL HUWA ALLAHU AHAD.`

Keep this one close: unique, the One a traveler loved too much to stop describing. Name sixty-seven, kept.

howItsDone: In each unit of prayer Muslims recite al-Fatiha and then other verses of the Qur'an; al-Ikhlas, being short, is a frequent choice, and children often learn it early.
